questions.text: What distinguishes full-duplex speech interaction from a system that strictly alternates listening and speaking?

options.A: It can receive user audio while producing its own audio.
options.B: It must finish transcribing the entire conversation before replying.
options.C: It uses one audio stream that switches direction after each turn.
options.D: It converts all audio into text and never produces speech.

questions.explanation: Full-duplex interaction keeps both incoming and outgoing audio streams active simultaneously, enabling interruptions and back-channeling.

questions.text: A low-latency dialogue model handles natural conversation but lacks reliable tool calling. Your assistant must execute validated calendar actions. Which design addresses that gap?

options.A: Treat generated speech as proof that the calendar action succeeded.
options.B: Reduce codec frame duration until tool execution emerges.
options.C: Integrate a separate tool-capable orchestration path with validated dispatch.
options.D: Replace tool schemas with speaker embeddings.

questions.explanation: Low-latency dialogue capability does not establish tool orchestration. A separate path can validate and dispatch actions and return actual results.

questions.text: The client creates mic_task and spk_task with asyncio.create_task, then awaits asyncio.gather(mic_task, spk_task). Both coroutines regularly await I/O. How do they run?

options.A: The microphone coroutine finishes before the speaker coroutine starts.
options.B: They run concurrently, yielding to each other while waiting for I/O.
options.C: They necessarily execute in two separate operating-system processes.
options.D: gather cancels the microphone task when speaker playback starts.

questions.explanation: Both tasks are scheduled on the event loop and can make progress while the other awaits I/O; this is concurrency, not an automatic separate-process guarantee.
